title: Right-of-Way
summary: Who must yield at intersections, stops, turns, driveways, crosswalks, roundabouts and merges, and what to do when someone else gets it wrong.

blocks.text: The law says who must yield. It never gives anyone the right to force their way through. Failing to yield puts two road users in the same space at the same time, which is how many crashes happen.

items: Even when you have the right-of-way, slow down or stop if another driver fails to yield. Avoiding a crash comes first.
Before you go, make sure the other driver is actually stopping or yielding to you.
If someone waves you on, check for traffic and pedestrians yourself before you move.
When you are not sure who should go first, yield and let the other driver go.

sections.heading: Intersections with no signs or signals

items: Slow down as you approach and be ready to stop for traffic from either side.
A vehicle already in the intersection goes first.
If two vehicles on different roads arrive at about the same time, the driver on the left yields to the driver on the right.
At a T-intersection, the driver on the road that ends yields to traffic on the through road.

blocks.text: A car on your right only goes first if it arrives at about the same time. A car still far away does not get to go first just because it is on your right. And if a car on your left should yield to you, be ready to stop in case it does not.

items: At a STOP sign where cross traffic does not stop, stop fully and yield to cross traffic and pedestrians before you go. Cars on the cross street have the right-of-way.
At a YIELD sign, traffic and pedestrians on the cross street go first.
At an all-way (four-way) stop, the first vehicle to stop goes first.
If two vehicles at right angles stop at the same time, the one on the right goes first. With cars on your left and right arriving together, the car on your right goes first.
Two drivers facing each other and both going straight may go at the same time.
If you are turning left and the driver facing you is going straight, they go first.
Even when it is your turn, stop fully and check for pedestrians. If another car rolls through without stopping, let it go.

blocks.text: When a traffic signal is dark because of a power outage, treat the intersection as an all-way stop. Drivers on the main road must stop too, and the same take-turns rules apply.

items: On a green light, you may go only after yielding to vehicles and pedestrians still in the intersection.
Turning left on a plain green light or a flashing yellow arrow, you yield to oncoming vehicles going straight or turning right.
Turning left into a driveway or alley mid-block, yield to oncoming traffic close enough to be a hazard.
On a green arrow, you still yield to vehicles and pedestrians already in the intersection.
Motorcycles are small, so their speed and distance are easy to misjudge. If unsure, yield.

sections.heading: Driveways, alleys, parking spaces and curbs

items: Leaving a driveway, alley or parking lot, yield to traffic on the street and to pedestrians on the sidewalk.
Turning left out of a lot onto a two-way street, yield to vehicles from both directions and to pedestrians.
Stop before the sidewalk when coming out of an alley or driveway, and wait for people walking by.
Pulling away from the curb, traffic already on the road goes first. Wait for a safe gap.
Backing out of a parking space, yield to vehicles and pedestrians passing behind you.
On the main road you have the right-of-way over a car waiting in a driveway, but watch in case it pulls out.

blocks.text: You must yield to pedestrians in both marked and unmarked crosswalks. An unmarked crosswalk is the crossing area at an intersection where no lines are painted.

items: Stop behind the crosswalk, at the stop line if there is one, so the whole crosswalk stays clear.
If a car in the next lane has stopped at a crosswalk, slow down and be ready to stop. Do not pass it; it may be stopped for someone you cannot see.
When turning on green, let pedestrians finish crossing the street you are turning onto.
If someone crosses mid-block outside a crosswalk, you must still slow down or stop to avoid hitting them.
Do not wave a pedestrian across a multilane road. A driver in another lane may not stop.

blocks.text: A person with a white cane or guide dog always gets the right-of-way, even if they start against the signal. Do not honk, which can confuse them, and do not stop in the crosswalk, which can force them to walk around your car into traffic. Quiet hybrid and electric cars are hard for them to hear, so take extra care.

Yield to any police car, fire truck, ambulance or other authorized emergency vehicle using its siren, flashing emergency lights, or both. Do not wait to both see lights and hear a siren before you move over.

items: Pull to the right edge of the road and stop. If traffic is heavy, move as far right as you safely can.
If you are already in an intersection, drive through it first, then pull right and stop.
Do not enter a roundabout while an emergency vehicle is approaching. If you are already in one, keep moving, exit, then pull over.
After it passes, check for more emergency vehicles before you move again.

blocks.text: A police car behind you with no siren or flashing lights does not require you to pull over. Rules for moving over or slowing down when passing stopped emergency vehicles vary by state; check your State Cheat Sheet.

items: Traffic in a U.S. roundabout moves counterclockwise, so look to your left before entering.
Yield to pedestrians in the crosswalk at the entry, then to traffic already in the roundabout, in all of its lanes. Yield to pedestrians in the exit crosswalk too.
Once you are inside, keep moving. Do not stop for cars waiting to enter unless you must to avoid a crash.
When you change lanes, a car already in that lane has the right-of-way.
When your lane ends, you must yield and merge into the next lane.
Merging from an on-ramp, highway traffic has the right-of-way. If no one makes room, adjust your speed and find a safe gap.

keyPoints: Right-of-way is given, not taken. Be ready to yield even when it is your turn.
With no signs or signals, vehicles already in the intersection go first; otherwise the driver on the left yields to the driver on the right.
At all-way stops the first to stop goes first; at a tie, the car on the right goes first.
Left-turning drivers yield to oncoming traffic and pedestrians.
Drivers entering from driveways, alleys, parking spaces or the curb yield to traffic and pedestrians.
Yield to pedestrians in marked and unmarked crosswalks, and always to a person with a white cane or guide dog.
For a siren or flashing emergency lights, pull to the right and stop, but clear an intersection first.
Entering a roundabout or merging, yield to the traffic already there.
